# Disagreement Log — T12_011 (Testament of Joseph)
**Chapter:** T12_011 | **Verses:** 9 sections (~20 verses)
**Translators compared:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA | **Arbiter:** SOPHIA

| # | Verse | Issue | EMET | LOGOS | PNEUMA | SOPHIA ruling |
|---|-------|-------|------|-------|--------|---------------|
| 1 | 1:5–7 | Antithetical catalogue | Full parallelism with colons | Same | Restructured as narrative list | EMET/LOGOS parallelism retained — this is the literary heart of the chapter; the antithetical rhythm must be preserved |
| 2 | 2:6 | "Ten temptations" | Present | Present | Omitted | "In ten temptations he showed me approved" retained — this is a known rabbinic motif (10 trials of Abraham applied to Joseph) |
| 3 | 3:5 | Fasting and beauty | "they-that-fast-for-God's-sake-receive-beauty-of-face" | Same | "God makes you look well-nourished even through fasting" | EMET/LOGOS literal preserved — this specific statement about fasting and divine beauty is theologically distinctive |
| 4 | 8:2 | "Lamb of God" | "Lamb-of-God, who-taketh-away-the-sin-of-the-world" | Same | "Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world" | All three agree; this is the most explicit Johannine anticipation in the Testaments — retained in all versions |
| 5 | 8:3 | Watcher's hammock image | "watcher's-hammock, which-after-the-summer-is-gone-is-seen-no-more" | Same | "field-watcher's shelter disappears after the summer harvest" | EMET/LOGOS "watcher's hammock" retained — the Greek skopian is a raised platform/shelter for watching fields; the image is precise and poignant |

---
*SOPHIA notes: Testament of Joseph is the theological climax of the Twelve. Joseph is the figure who suffered most and forgave most — and his testimony is deliberately structured as an antithetical hymn (1:5–7). The "Lamb of God who taketh away the sin of the world" (8:2) is the most overt NT anticipation in the entire corpus — all three translators flag it implicitly, and SOPHIA retains without insertion. The "watcher's hammock" (8:3) is a unique image — the temporary field shelter, gone after harvest, is Joseph's image for the transience of earthly kingdoms. This Testament is also unique in that both sons AND brothers are addressed (1:2) — Joseph speaks to the whole family.*
